concept.name: Carhart four-factor model
concept.definition: An extension of the Fama-French three-factor model introduced by Mark Carhart (1997, 'On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance') that adds a momentum factor - long stocks with high prior 2-12 month returns and short those with low prior returns - to the market, size, and value factors.
concept.intuition: To judge a fund fairly you must also control for whether it was simply riding recent winners, because momentum explains much of what looked like persistent skill.
concept.mechanics: R_i - R_f = alpha_i + b_i*(R_m - R_f) + s_i*SMB + h_i*HML + m_i*Mom + e_i. Carhart used the Jegadeesh-Titman momentum factor (top minus bottom decile of prior 12-2 month returns); the standard data-library Mom variant averages the high-minus-low prior-return spread across small and big value-weight portfolios.
concept.formula: R_i - R_f = alpha_i + b_i*(R_m - R_f) + s_i*SMB + h_i*HML + m_i*Mom + e_i, with Mom = (1/2)(Small High + Big High) - (1/2)(Small Low + Big Low) on prior (2-12) returns.
concept.failure_modes: The momentum leg exposes the model to momentum crashes in sharp market reversals, and alpha rankings of funds can flip depending on whether momentum is included; like all such models it is an empirical benchmark, not a theory of required returns.
concept.misconceptions: Carhart's key finding was that much apparent mutual-fund performance persistence disappears after controlling for momentum and expenses - the four-factor alpha, not raw return rank, is the meaningful persistence measure.
concept.example: Evaluating a growth-fund manager, a three-factor regression shows 2% alpha; adding the momentum factor reveals a large positive Mom loading and shrinks alpha toward zero, showing the 'skill' was largely momentum exposure.
